question: Between 2010 and 2021, France had the highest number of attacks in Europe (5), followed by Germany (3) and Sweden (2). Austria, Denmark, Hungary, Belgium and Spain reported one attack each. A decade of jihadist attacks in France culminated with the Islamist barbarism of 7, 8 and 9 January 2015. In Paris and Montrouge, 17 people were murdered with weapons of war in the name of Allah.

Other horrors had preceded the attacks, such as the despicable murder of three children at the Ozar Hatorah school1 in Toulouse in 2012. Other disgraceful acts followed, such as the Bataclan attack in Paris on 13 November 2015.

As we enter 2025, which – appallingly – marks 10 years of Islamist crimes against the French people, with many other European countries having suffered similar acts of violence, Europeans are still at risk from Islamism. 1.
What commemorative steps has the Commission taken to pay tribute to the victims of Islamist attacks in Europe since 2010, in particular those that took place in France in 2015?
As we mark 10 years since the 2015 attacks, what is the assessment of the risk of Islamist terrorism in Europe?
How does the Commission support Member States in the face of Islamist violence?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.3.2025) 1. Since 2004, the Commission organises on 11 March the European Remembrance Day for Victims of Terrorism. This event was established in the aftermath of the terrorist attacks in Madrid on 11 March 2004.

Its purpose is to remember and to support victims of terrorist attacks by providing them with a platform to gather, share their stories and experiences and, in turn, for them to hear about EU collaborative efforts to prevent and counter terrorism and support victims in their needs. It is also an opportunity to highlight the important role that victims can play in preventing violent radicalisation.

In the last years, French victims and survivors of terrorism have attended the ceremony and given their testimony. In 2025, which marks 10 years since the Charlie Hebdo and Bataclan attacks, the event will be held in Strasbourg to pay tribute to the victims of terrorism in France and throughout Europe. 2.

The Commission relies on threat assessments produced by the EU Intelligence and Situation Centre of the EU Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol)1 as well as information shared by the Member States. In the current security landscape, the Islamist terrorist threat remains high in the EU. 3. While national security is a competence of Member States2, the Commission supports Member States to counter terrorism.

Considering the high and fast evolving security threat in the EU, the Commission is currently preparing a new Internal Security Strategy and a new Agenda on Preventing and Countering Terrorism and Violent Extremism3, both to be published in 2025. The Commission will also propose to strengthen Europol, whose mandate was already reinforced in 20224.
Furthermore, the Commission has established the EU Knowledge Hub on Prevention of Radicalisation5 to support Member States in their prevention efforts.
